title: Rav Huna, Alleged Father of Rabbi Ze’ira HaKohen
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman regards this as an invented Amora. The error came from Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 8:5, which reads: “Abba bar bar Chana and Rav Chuna were sitting and eating, and Rabbi Ze’ira was standing and serving before them … Abba bar bar Chana said to him, ‘Is your other hand cut off?’ … and his father was angry with him and said: ‘Is it not enough for you that you are reclining and he is standing serving? And moreover he is a Kohen!’ … and he decreed that Rabbi Zeira should sit and he would serve.” Seder HaDorot built a great argument from this as to whether Rabbi Zeira was the son of Abba bar bar Chana or of Rav Huna; Hyman rejects this and develops Penei Moshe’s explanation: Abba bar bar Chana and Bar Chana (Hyman proposes this instead of Rav Chuna) sat down to eat, and Rabbi Zeira stood and served before them. Abba bar bar Chana said to Rabbi Zeira, “Is your other hand cut off?” and his father — that is, Bar Chana — was angry with his son and said to him: “But Rabbi Zeira is a Kohen!” (as explained in his entry), and therefore he decreed that Rabbi Zeira should sit and he would serve before them.

The Yalkut, Ezra, remez 1069, cites a reading Hyman endorses: Abba (he is Rabbah) and Rav Huna sat down to eat, and Rabbi Ze’ira was serving before them. The explanation is likewise as Hyman explains, but there it became corrupted at the end; see the entry Rabbah bar bar Chana.

notes.text: Saved Guggenheimer English Berakhot8:5 has Is your other hand cut off? The former white-hand rendering omitted the cut-off predicate. Hyman’s rejection of a Huna-as-father figure, proposed Bar Chana substitution and alternative Yalkut account remain his arguments; the title marks the rejected fatherhood as alleged, without deleting the source notice.

The consulted Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 8:5 directly preserves Abba bar bar Chana, Rav Chuna, the cut-off-hand question and the priest-service rebuke. It does not itself settle which figure the father is. Hyman’s Bar Chana substitution, rejection of the alleged father notice and Yalkut interpretation remain his arguments.
